newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Dec 27.

text.p: A man was killed attempting to parachute from a bluff at Fox Glacier yesterday, as his fiancee and a friend watched in horror from below. The 29-year-old man jumped to his death minutes after the bluff had nearly claimed the life of his companion parachutist. Page 1.

The Justice Ministry has warned that New Zealand's obligations under international treaties have limited the scope of local law. In its post-election briefing papers to the incoming government, the ministry echoes concerns raised by Clerk of the House David McGee, who said earlier this year that international treaty negotiations were "undemocratic" as few New Zealanders were aware of what was being negotiated on these treaties, many of which were binding on New Zealand. The ministry says joining international treaties -- such as the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade -- is an "executive act" involving only ministers and officials. Page 2.

The Justice Ministry has commissioned a study to see if New Zealand experiences about crime match those of people overseas. In its post-election briefing papers to the incoming government, the ministry says victim surveys carried out in Britain, Australia, and the United States showed that crimes reported to the police were only a small proportion of the actual crime figures. Page 2.

A tourist and a boy have drowned and a scuba diver is dead after incidents during the holiday period. The body of Invercargill boy Vijay Simon Jeet, 12, who fell into the Manawatu River on Christmas Day, was found by police divers yesterday about 250 metres downstream from where he went missing. A German tourist drowned when he tried to swim across the Rangitikei River near Mangaweka on Christmas Eve. Page 3.

The euro-kiwi market has ended the year with a bang with a NZ$200 million offering of five year eurobonds from the World Bank. Despite the end-of-year timing, syndicate manager Toronto Dominion Bank said that virtually all the issue was sold immediately after launch, bar a small position, which Tor-Dom would manage during the holiday season. "It's been a surprisingly stunning year for the New Zealand dollar market," a syndicate manager at Toronto Dominion Bank, lead underwriter for the World Bank issue, said. "We've seen extremely strong demand. The New Zealand dollar has a much more global base than either Canadian dollars or Australian dollars." Page 11.

The worst is past for the economy with strong growth forecast for the next two years, the National Bank says. The bank's forecasts for January say growth should be about 3.5 percent in each of the next two years, while inflation will fall to one percent over the next year before beginning to rise again in 1998. The exchange rate will fall but not by the 10 percent to 15 percent many are hoping for, the bank says. Page 11.

Christmas ward closures at Auckland Hospital will be extended, forcing patients already queing for surgery to wait even longer. Two wards traditionally shut down over the holiday were due to reopen by mid-January. But the prospect of a budget blowout of at least NZ$3 million from surgery numbers of urgent cases has seen officials cut back on elective operations. Page 1.

As many as 25,000 New Zealand families -- five percent of the total -- may be caught in a cycle of serious disadvantage, estimates the Ministry of Education. And it says many of them live in South Auckland, which has 37 of the most socially and economically disadvantaged schools in the country. Page 1.

Apple grower Grocorp Pacific is urging the New Zealand Apple and Pear Marketing Board to strive for operational efficiencies to improve returns to growers. Net returns an export carton received from the board were, for Grocorp, below those of 1995, the managing director, Ross Johnson, says in the annual report.
Last year the company received an average of about $12 a carton, down from $18 in 1994.

New Zealand Salmon Company's directors expect an early return to profit for the business. The Christchurch-based salmon farmer booked a bottom-line loss of $1.55 million in the year to September 30, attributed to weak market prices. In the annual report, they say they are aware of the problems in the salmon market caused by increased production in Chile and Norway. However, cost efficiencies and the species mix of Aquacultivos, the company's 50 percent joint venture in Chile, was considered to be better than that of many of its competitors.

Tower Corporation is moving from a passive to an active position on demutualisation. The chairman, Colin Beyer, said the former Government Life was the last of the main superannuation and insurance mutual societies in Australia and New Zealand to deal with demutualisation. AMP, Colonial Mutual and National Mutual had all either demutualised or were in the process.

Finance company Dorchester Pacific hopes to cut costs by reducing the size of its share register. The company said in October that it spent around $400,000 a year complying with New Zealand Stock Exchange listing requirements. That compared with a March-year after-tax profit of $270,000. About 1,500 shareholders own less than 2,000 shares, and those parcels are worth less than $200 at the current price. Those shareholders must top up their holdings to at least 2000 by buying shares on the market, or sell their holding. If they have not done so by March 19, Dorchester will buy their shares compulsorily, under the Companies Act.

Air New Zealand and Fletcher Paper are the stocks most favoured by sharebrokers to perform in 1997. Of the 12 brokers asked by the New Zealand Herald to pick their top stocks for the coming year, five put both companies on their shortlist. Otherwise, the picks were varied, with 31 different stocks chosen among their five selections. Most brokers based their picks around an expected weakening in the New Zealand dollar and falling interest rates, which are not expect to track back up until late 1997. This, for example, saw the likes of fishing company Sanford feature by being included in three picks. It is the second year Air New Zealand has taken top billing. Last year, it shared the most favoured status with Telecom, which falls into second spot.
